Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Military Medic
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

Vignette:
Michael O’Shea, a 45-year-old military medic, still wears the same desert combat boots he had on three years ago when the earthquake hit. He isn’t sure why he can’t let them go. They remind him of something, but he cannot put the memories of that day in the right order—only fragments that rush back with the same sickening terror he felt then, and when they do, he has to stop whatever he is doing or he will shake apart.

The earthquake struck during a routine rotation at a forward operating base in a coastal region. Michael had just finished a morning sick call when the ground lurched. He remembers the sound first—a deep, grinding roar, like the earth was tearing itself apart. After that, the images come in a flood, jumbled: a concrete wall buckling, dust so thick he could not see his hands, a young airman trapped under a support beam, screaming. He worked for hours, prying debris with his bare hands, trying to keep the man talking until extraction arrived. He remembers the man’s name was Riley, but the sequence of events before and after is a smear. He remembers Riley going quiet. He remembers a second aftershock that nearly buried them both. He remembers walking out of the rubble at dusk, covered in other people’s blood, and feeling nothing at all.

That changed. Within weeks, Michael could not shake the feeling that the world had become a place where the ground could fall away without warning. He started to startle at any unexpected or loud sound—a dropped pan, a helicopter overhead, even a door slamming in the barracks. His heart would hammer, and he would scan the room as if ready to dive for cover. He knew he was safe; the base had been rebuilt, the drills were over. But his body did not know. He could not relax, not even in his own quarters at night, because his ears kept straining for the next crack, the next shudder.

His work suffered. As a medic, he had always been steady in a crisis; now he found himself avoiding the trauma bay when he could, inventing reasons to stay in the supply closet. The loud clatter of medical instruments being sterilised sent him into a cold sweat. He stopped making eye contact with patients. The job that used to give his life meaning felt hollow. Nothing seemed meaningful anymore—not the men he was supposed to treat, not the letters his wife had written him before she died of cancer two years before the quake. He had once believed in the order of things: that if you worked hard and kept your head, you could make a difference. That belief had been destroyed. The earthquake had shown him that chaos could swallow anyone, and he had been helpless. He felt like he did not know himself anymore. The calm, competent medic was gone. In his place was a man who flinched at a cough and lay awake staring at the ceiling, listening for aftershocks that would never come.

The avoidance spread. He stopped going to the mess hall at peak hours because the roar of conversation sounded too much like the noise after the collapse. He declined invitations to play cards with his old unit, claiming fatigue. His commanding officer noticed the change and suggested he take leave, but being home alone was worse—the quiet made him jump at the creak of the house settling. He had come to believe that the ground, or something, was always about to betray him.

What finally brought him to the clinic was an accidental blast of the base’s outdoor warning siren during a maintenance test. The sound hit him like a physical blow. He dropped to his knees in the middle of the parade ground, gasping, convinced the demolition was starting again. Two fellow medics carried him inside. That night, he called the chaplain and asked for a referral. He is terrified that he is losing his mind, that he will never be the man his wife once knew, that the memories will never stop feeling as fresh as the moment they happened. But he is also afraid to hope that talking about them could change any of that.
